rv.q: “For all the detailed behavior that shows up at the surface — the various ways the women sip from their water bottles, the shuffling or striding or creeping to their chaises — you always sense the greater weight of whatever lies beneath.
From the name onward, nothing in Annie Baker’s fearless new play Infinite Life is laboriously explained; everything is prismlike and expansive.

Here and throughout the play, Ms. Baker indicates that, contrary to the Hallmarky cliché, no one can feel another’s pain, even when her characters do their best to describe it or evoke its effects, as when Eileen says, “A minute of this is an infinity.”
But the levity and weirdness vibrate at a low frequency, and the Annie Baker seesaw feels treacherously out of whack.
Annie Baker’s riveting new play explores the way in which inner life transcends pain and the limitations of the body
Pain may be trapped in the sufferer’s body, but great acting in such primal, honest drama can soothe a collective hurt.

So it is a fitting if amusing testament to Baker’s dogged uncertainty that her riveting new play Infinite Life, which opens tonight at the Atlantic Theater Company (in a co-production with London’s National Theatre), includes a Christian Scientist character who is experiencing a crisis of faith.
Among our playwrights, only Baker can illuminate such transient episodes with such feeling and insight.
Each is an intricate part of Baker’s gorgeous mosaic of tribulations and coping mechanisms.
A seemingly effortless overlaying of the transcendent and the mundane is the elusive and enrapturing touch of Annie Baker...
Baker infuses this new work with signature humor, humanity, and feels-so-real dialogue.
For those who like a theatrical challenge, the play minutely focuses attention on the mundane and the prosaic.

Baker's rendering of her characters' experience of pain and illness—or rather her rendering of their attempts to capture those experiences in language—is blazingly visceral, especially in those pauses.
Infinite Life has much to say about the ideas it explores, and it does so with laser-sharp exactitude.
I suspect many people will forget – or try to forget – this often-unpleasant play the second they re-emerge on 20th Street.
Baker deserves much thanks for that.
Those rewards felt fewer this time around.
Much of it will certainly resonate, especially with audiences of a certain age, and Baker leavens the grimness of the proceedings with frequent dashes of deadpan mordant humor.
It is the kind of play that people will be talking about for a long, long time.
Baker can also be a poet of the revolting, such as when Nelson matter-of-factly describes the sensation of defecating out of his mouth.

cn.t: Baker's contemplative character study of chronic pain patients at a California clinic divides critics with its signature slow pace and pauses, though most praise the emotional depth, humor, and exceptional ensemble performances.
